newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Weak techs see Australia bonds overshoot U.S..
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Weak techs see Australia bonds overshoot U.S..

text.p: *Weakening technicals on Australian bond futures saw the market overshoot Thursday's sharp sell-off in U.S. Treasuries.
*Although the market gets its first major data of the year next week, action in the U.S. is likely to dominate.
A weakening technical picture saw Australian bond futures fall further during the afternoon and the market overshoot Thursday's sharp sell-off in U.S. debt.

Long-dated yields spiked to their highest level since mid-October, although turnover remained relatively light following the year-end holidays which tended to exaggerate price movements, traders said.
"It's all been futures driven. Nothing has changed here fundamentally to warrant current levels," one trader added.
However, one saving grace for the market next week could be the return of Japanese investors after a week long holiday.
"As long as the U.S. behaves itself, the market could now provide buying opportunities, particularly from Japan," the trader added.

However, it is the uncertainty over the outlook of the U.S. which has given domestic bonds a nasty jolt in the first few days of the year, with long yields there having risen 20 basis points in the last two trading sessions.

The latest spike on Thursday followed an unexpected jump in the December U.S. NAPM index to 54.0 and just short of the 55.0 level which historically has preceded tightenings in monetary policy by the Federal Reserve.
Although the domestic market gets its first major data of the week, action in the U.S. is likely to be the dominating factor in the near term.
The U.S. releases the December PPI next Thursday and the key non-farm payrolls report for the same month on Friday.

"Any hint in these numbers that U.S. economic activity may be picking up speed and/or price pressures may be building would see some further solid selling in U.S. Treasuries as market anxiety would mount...that the Fed may be back in tightening mode in the first half of 1997," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Group.
Local weakness saw long-dated spreads blow out sharply against the U.S. and reverse an early tightening against Canada and New Zealand.
The domestic market faces November balance of payments on Monday, and building approvals and retail trade on Tuesday.

The early break of 92.340 on the 10-year contract, which represented a 50 percent retracement of the September/December, set the weak tone in motion. A further barrier at 92.270 was also severed, leaving the market testing key support at 92.210.
